title: Third-Line Overactive Bladder Therapies on TikTok: What Does the Public Learn?
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of TikTok videos on third-line overactive bladder (OAB) therapies. The abstract reports a quantitative share of items classified as containing misinformation with an explicit denominator (22/119 included videos, 18.4%), coded by two reviewers. That satisfies the CONTENT criterion. The MQ-VET quality scores are reported only as medians, so they yield no additional row.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language TikTok; author affiliation not given in the abstract)
estimates.date: not stated in the abstract (cross-sectional analysis of the top 50 videos per keyword)
estimates.measure_type: % of included TikTok videos on third-line OAB therapies that contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: 119 TikTok videos included after screening the top 50 videos for each of 6 OAB third-line therapy keywords (300 videos screened)
estimates.definition: Two reviewers determined whether the video contained misinformation; recurring misinformation themes were therapy indication, mechanism of action, and patient limitations after undergoing therapy
estimates.misinfo_def: no explicit definition given in the abstract; 'Two reviewers determined if videos contained misinformation.'
estimates.source_quote: Twenty-two videos (18.4%) contained misinformation, which were 3 times longer (50.5 vs 15 seconds, P < 0.01) and had higher MQ-VET scores (34.5 vs 27, P = 0.03) than those without misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two reviewers judged the presence of misinformation (video-level, against clinical knowledge of third-line OAB therapies); quality was separately scored by 3 independent reviewers with the Medical Quality Video Evaluation Tool (MQ-VET). No inter-rater reliability statistic and no external ground-truth document are reported in the abstract.
estimates.moderator_quote: In this cross-sectional analysis, we abstracted the top 50 TikTok videos for keywords: "Axonics," "sacral neuromodulation," "Interstim," "PTNS," "posterior tibial nerve stimulation," and "bladder Botox." Videos were scored for quality by 3 independent reviewers using the Medical Quality Video Evaluation Tool (MQ-VET). Two reviewers determined if videos contained misinformation.
estimates.notes: denom_selection=curated because the sample is a rank-truncated top-50-per-keyword set. denom_scope=topical (single clinical topic). No data-collection date or publication year appears anywhere in the abstract-only text, so year is left blank rather than guessed. The misinformation judgement is distinct from the MQ-VET quality score, so the row is CONTENT and not QUALITY.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Creator-type subgroup misinformation rates ('no difference in the rate of misinformation between MP and non-MP videos (21% vs 18%)') were not extracted: they are subgroup splits of the headline 18.4%, are rounded, and their denominators (24 medical-professional vs 95 other videos) are not given alongside the percentages. (2) MQ-VET quality scores are reported only as medians (43 vs 27; 34.5 vs 27), i.e. scale means with no share of items, so per the instructions no QUALITY row is created. (3) 'Twenty-four (21%) were created by medical professionals' is a share of creators, not of misinformation, so it is not an estimate. (4) Whole-text verification was impossible: this is an abstract-only record.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis; sampling frame = top 50 TikTok videos per each of 6 keywords (300 screened, 119 included, exclusions not itemised in the abstract); misinformation coded by two reviewers, quality by three reviewers with MQ-VET; no inter-rater reliability, no adjudication procedure and no data-collection date reported in the abstract-only text.
rob.item6_quote: Two reviewers determined if videos contained misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: Of 300 videos screened, 119 videos were included. ... Twenty-two videos (18.4%) contained misinformation
